title: Risk Management
description: How to protect an organization's assets with limited time and budget: value the assets, analyze the risks, treat them, and use a framework to manage the process.

nodes.title: 1. Asset Valuation
nodes.description:
Step 1: give each asset a value, so assets can be ranked from most to least valuable.
Simple in concept, hard in practice.

children.title: Quantitative
children.description:
Give each asset a monetary value.
The preferred method in principle, but usually not possible with reasonable accuracy. For most assets, such as reputation or a data set, you cannot assign an exact monetary value.

children.title: Qualitative
children.description:
Rank assets relative to each other, often with categories such as high, medium and low value.
Used most of the time, because monetary values are usually impossible to determine.

nodes.title: 2. Risk Analysis
nodes.description: Step 2: identify the risks to each asset by looking at threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood and impact, then rank the risks.

children.title: Threats
children.description:
Any potential danger: events, situations or actions that can harm assets, operations or reputation.
Sources include natural disasters, cyber attacks, fraud, theft and human error.

children.title: Threat Modeling
children.description:
Structured methods to identify and analyze threats systematically.
The three to know are STRIDE, PASTA and DREAD.

children.title: STRIDE
children.description:
Identifies threats. Quick and easy, but not very thorough.
Sorts threats into six categories: pretending to be someone else, changing data without permission, denying having done an action, leaking information, making a service unavailable, and gaining privileges you should not have.

children.title: PASTA
children.description:
A seven-step, risk-centric method that simulates attacks to analyze threats. Time-consuming and in-depth.
Considers the business value of assets and compliance, and gives a strategic threat analysis with more useful results than the quick six-category method.
Full name: Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis.

children.title: DREAD
children.description:
Does not identify threats: it prioritizes threats that are already identified.
Often used with STRIDE: STRIDE finds the threats, DREAD ranks them.
Rates each threat on five factors: the damage it could do, how easily the attack can be repeated, how easily it can be exploited, how many users would be affected, and how easily the weakness can be found.

children.title: Vulnerabilities
children.description: A weakness or gap in security or controls that a threat can exploit to harm assets, operations or reputation.

children.title: Vuln. Assessment & Pen. Testing
children.description:
Two techniques to find weaknesses systematically:
- scanning and reviewing systems to find and list known weaknesses
- simulating real attacks to find which weaknesses can actually be exploited
Covered in detail in its own mind map in Domain 6.

children.title: Likelihood
children.description: The probability that a risk event will happen.

children.title: Impact
children.description:
The harm or damage to the organization if the risk happens.
Examples: downtime, damage to reputation, data integrity problems, a breach, ransomware.

children.title: Quantitative
children.description:
Calculate how much a risk will cost the organization per year.
Useful to decide which controls are worth their cost.
The inputs are usually impossible to determine accurately, so ranking risks relative to each other is used most of the time.

children.title: ALE = SLE(Value x Exposure) x ARO
children.description:
Know this formula for the exam.
- ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) = SLE x ARO: the expected loss per year.
- SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) = Asset Value x Exposure Factor: the loss if the risk happens once.
- Exposure Factor: the percentage of the asset expected to be lost. 10% means a tenth of the asset is lost; 100% means all of it.
- ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence): how many times per year the risk is expected to happen. Once a year is 1; five times a year is 5.

children.title: Qualitative
children.description:
Rank risks relative to each other.
Not great, but much better than nothing.

nodes.title: 3. Treatment
nodes.description: Step 3: decide how to respond to each risk. There are four ways: avoid, transfer, mitigate or accept.

children.title: Avoid
children.description:
Stop the risk from happening, or do not do the activity that causes it.
Example: do not jump out of an airplane without a parachute.

children.title: Transfer
children.description:
Move the financial burden to someone else, for example by buying insurance.
You can never transfer accountability. The insurer does not become accountable for the risk.

children.title: Mitigate
children.description:
Reduce the risk with controls. Security professionals spend most of their time here.
No set of controls removes a risk completely. The risk left after the controls are in place is the residual risk.

children.title: Administrative
children.description:
Controls made of policies, procedures and other organizational practices.
Examples: security policies, employee training and awareness.

children.title: Technical / Logical
children.description:
Controls made of technology.
Examples: firewalls, intrusion detection systems, encryption, automated backups.

children.title: Physical
children.description:
Controls in the physical world.
Examples: fences, cameras, locks, fire suppression systems.

children.title: Safeguards
children.description: Controls that try to stop a risk from happening.

children.title: Directive
children.description:
Tell people how to behave and how to handle risks.
Example: policies.

children.title: Deterrent
children.description:
Discourage people from risky or harmful behavior. They discourage; they do not prevent.
Example: a warning sign on private property.

children.title: Preventative
children.description:
Stop a risk from happening.
Examples: fences topped with razor wire, login mechanisms, firewalls.

children.title: Countermeasures
children.description: Controls that detect and respond to a risk that has already happened.

children.title: Detective
children.description:
Identify risks that have happened or are happening.
Examples: SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) systems, intrusion detection systems, smoke detectors.

children.title: Corrective
children.description:
Reduce the damage after a risk has happened.
Example: a fire suppression system that puts out a fire.

children.title: Recovery
children.description:
Help the organization recover and get back to business as usual.
Example: a Disaster Recovery Plan (DRP).

children.title: Compensating
children.description: Reduce the damage when other controls are not effective or not possible. They make up for the lack of a better control.

children.title: Functional
children.description:
Every good control has two aspects. The functional aspect is what the control is meant to do.
Example: a firewall controls the traffic between network segments.

children.title: Assurance
children.description:
The second aspect of a good control: being able to confirm that it keeps working correctly over time.
Example: logging and monitoring a firewall.

children.title: Accept
children.description:
A deliberate decision to accept a level of risk and its consequences.
The asset owner should accept the risk, because the owner is accountable for the asset and best placed to decide.

nodes.title: Risk Frameworks
nodes.description: Structured, systematic approaches to managing risk.

children.title: RMF (NIST 800-37)
children.description:
The US federal government's seven-step process to manage risks to information systems and data.
Know the seven steps and their order at a high level:
1. Prepare: get ready to manage risk at the organization and system levels.
2. Categorize: categorize systems and identify the risks.
3. Select: choose controls for the identified risks.
4. Implement: put the controls in place.
5. Assess: check that the controls are effective.
6. Authorize: based on the assessment, a senior official (the authorizing official) decides whether the risk is acceptable and the system can go into production.
7. Monitor: keep checking that the controls work in production.
Full name: Risk Management Framework.

children.title: ISO 31000
children.description: An international standard that gives principles and guidelines for managing any type of risk in any organization. Recognize the name.

children.title: COSO
children.description: An enterprise risk management framework focused on internal control and corporate governance. It grew out of US work on fraudulent financial reporting (the Treadway Commission). Recognize the name.

children.title: ISACA Risk IT
children.description: A framework for managing IT-related business risk, from the professional association that also publishes COBIT. Recognize the name.
